lesson_title: How a Democracy Voted Itself Off
hook_text: The Nazis never won a majority in a free election. So how did Hitler become dictator in 18 months?
clip_script: July 1932. The Nazis win 37 percent. The biggest party, but not a majority. November, they drop to 33. Then a back-door deal. Conservative politicians think they can use Hitler's voters and keep him on a leash. 30 January 1933, President Hindenburg makes Hitler chancellor. Only three Nazis in the cabinet. Four weeks later, the parliament building burns. Hitler blames the communists. Next day, an emergency decree wipes out free speech, free newspapers, and protection from arrest. Thousands are locked up. Then, 23 March 1933. Parliament meets in an opera house, stormtroopers lining the walls, communist members already arrested. The Enabling Act: let the government make laws without parliament. 444 votes for. 94 against. Parliament switched itself off. By July, every other party is banned. By August 1934, Hitler is Führer. Democracy does not always die in one blow. Sometimes it votes for its own end, under threat.
visual_style: Election bars rise to 37 percent and stop below a 50 percent line; a door creaks open labelled 30 January 1933; flames over a domed parliament; a vote counter ticks to 444 to 94 as shadows of uniformed men line a hall; a light switch flips off.
pacing: Steady build through 1932, a sharp turn at the fire, slow and heavy on the vote, quiet close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for who voted Nazi, the Enabling Act and how the dictatorship was built.
